t: Shift Distance Between Two Strings — Circular Prefix Costs
o: Each position of s must become the corresponding letter of t; shifting forward from letter a costs nextCost summed over visited letters, backward costs previousCost likewise, wrapping around the alphabet. Per position the cheapest direction is independent of other positions, so the answer is a sum of 26-independent minima. Example 2 ('leet'->'code') costs 9+10+1+11 = 31. With |s| up to 1e5 and costs up to 1e9, prefix sums over the doubled 26-cycle answer each pair in O(1).
k: Positions are independent: total cost = sum over i of minCost(s[i] -> t[i]).
Prefix sums of nextCost (clockwise) and previousCost (counter-clockwise) give both directional costs for any letter pair in O(1).

a.i: For each (a, b) pair, walk at most 25 steps in each direction accumulating costs and take the cheaper. O(26n) total — simple and passes comfortably, and needs no precomputation.
s: For each index, let a = s[i], b = t[i].
Walk forward a -> b adding nextCost, walk backward adding previousCost.
Add the minimum to the answer.
a.t: O(26n) — at most 25 steps per direction per character.

a.i: Build nc[i] = sum of nextCost[0..i-1] and pc[i] = sum of previousCost[0..i-1], each of length 27. Clockwise cost from a to b (a<b) is nc[b]-nc[a], wrapping via nc[26]-nc[a]+nc[b]; counter-clockwise is symmetric with pc. Each pair is then O(1).
s: For each (a, b): if equal, cost 0; else compute both directional formulas.
a.t: O(n + 26) — prefix construction plus one O(1) evaluation per character.

w: Use prefix sums in an interview; mention that mixing directions mid-route never helps because costs are additive per edge and each cycle position is crossed in one direction optimally. Pitfalls: the a == b case (cost 0), wrap-around off-by-ones (previous shift from 'a' charges previousCost[0]), and totals up to ~2.6e15 requiring 64-bit types. Follow-up: what if you could shift a whole substring at once, or costs depended on the target letter too?
